doc.title: Larry Gold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2025

title: Editing strings in Berlin and open voicing
summary: Gold edited an over-written arrangement for a string session, and defines his open, quartet-like voicings.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Very interesting. I watched the other, this was fascinating you were in Berlin, 2018 I think, and it was a video of working with a string section and it looked like it was the first read through of what you had — I think you wrote the chart.
I didn't write the chart. I remember it.

Okay. I wonder then, because of some things you said but here's a couple of comments you made during that session to the string players. First of all, "You've got to wait." They kept coming in early on like the and of four or something, and then you said, "don't overplay" because they were just I guess really getting into it. And then you said I thought significantly, "you don't need that."

Yeah. I edited his arrangement. I went in to the control room and asked them if I could. Because they had over—written it you know? And I sort of edited it. And the string players, you know if you stayed there for an hour or two hours they would have gotten it even the way he wrote it. But the thing is why? You know? It was not necessary. So I very kindly asked him if I could edit. And he consented that. Yeah. But yeah I mean I really — you have all these microphones and you have all these things, I mean it's good to play forte all the time and show me how you can play, but the thing is is I'm more interested in the mood of the record and how the record sounds, and how the violin sounds. You know when I — or how the cello sounds. You know? I mean when I feel myself pressing either on the cello I don't like it. You know it's a tight sound. It's not an open sound. And I like an open sound. I like things to have an openness to them, in the same way that I — when I write chords I like open chords. I like — I don't like dense things. I like more things that are — it depends on the song but most of the time I like more of an open voicing.
Define — what is your version of open voicing?

My version of open voicing is almost like a string quartet. So the cello has a note, the viola has a note and the violin might have two notes or maybe three notes. It's not like eight notes. I mean there are arrangers that come in and I — the violins are stacked you know. And it's not — I'm not saying it's bad, it's just not the way I write.
Like a little air in there.
Big time. More than a little.

I think it's interesting that you talk about volume and playing really hard because you could say well play as loud as you want, we'll just pull the bar down of your volume but that's not how it works. You're still going to get loud playing softer. © Fillius Jazz Archive 8
